final.uncertainty: The actual demand for safety-oriented marine coatings among individual buyers is unknown. The test will provide data on purchase intent and price sensitivity, but it does not confirm market size or willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the test shows the Protection-focused condition achieving a higher purchase intent score than the Safety-focused condition by at least 5 points, the recommendation would shift to a protection-focused proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two conditions, further market research would be needed to understand consumer motivations.

arguments.name: Safety vs Protection Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Safety-focused (emphasizing marine safety hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Protection-focused (emphasizing protection from marine elements and chemical damage). After viewing the message, participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: Proposed sample: 500 participants (250 per condition) from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Protection-focused condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Protection-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Safety-focused condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Safety-focused condition is at least 5 points higher than the Protection-focused condition (i.e., Safety ≥ Protection + 5), proceed with a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, proceed with a protection‑focused proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

After viewing the page, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase (functional need, status/prestige, or other).
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in purchase intent.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary purchase reason (functional need, status/prestige, other).

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, not just speculate.
Consider existing consumer reach of Jotun’s coatings; if none, assess feasibility of entering that market.
Alternatives include expanding into consumer markets, targeting a different customer group, or maintaining current B2B focus.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential marine safety, outdoor equipment protection) using Jotun’s marine technology.
2) Expand into consumer markets without a differentiated proposition, targeting individual buyers directly with existing coatings.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on B2B shipyards, ship owners, and industrial customers.
4) Partner with or license Jotun’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own brand.

X1.name: Safety vs Trust Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Safety Condition (safety-focused messaging emphasizing marine hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Trust Condition (trust-focused messaging emphasizing Jotun's brand reputation and existing procurement patterns for commercial buildings). Both conditions present the same product (Jotun marine protective coating) at a fixed price point. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from a panel of homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Trust Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trust Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Safety Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in the Safety Condition exceeds the Trust Condition by at least 10% (EUR), conclude T1 is supported. If the Trust Condition exceeds the Safety Condition by at least 10%, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10%, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.

The evidence shows Jotun already offers direct-to-consumer sales and has a consumer distribution network, but there is no direct evidence that individual buyers purchase for safety reasons. Conduct the proposed Safety vs Trust Messaging Test to validate whether safety‑f
final.target_customer: Homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts in Scandinavia who own boats, yachts, and recreational vehicles and are concerned about marine safety and durability.
final.value_proposition: Position Jotun’s marine technology as a safety solution for marine and outdoor protection, offering premium-priced products and direct-to-consumer sales through the brand website, with safety-focused messaging to justify the premium.
final.next_action: Run the Safety vs Trust Messaging Test (300 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under safety and trust messaging conditions.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for marine safety products and whether individual buyers are willing to pay a premium for safety-related coatings remain uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the Safety Condition fails to show a 10% higher willingness to pay than the Trust Condition, the investment case would weaken and we would reconsider the consumer proposition.
If additional evidence shows strong consumer demand for marine safety products or that trust alone drives purchases, we would explore a trust‑focused proposition.
If the test results show no significant difference between the two conditions, we would recommend maintaining the current B2B focus.

arguments.name: Safety vs Trust Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Safety Condition (safety-focused messaging emphasizing marine hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Trust Condition (trust-focused messaging emphasizing Jotun's brand reputation and existing procurement patterns for commercial buildings). Both conditions present the same product (Jotun marine protective coating) at a fixed price point. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from a panel of homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Trust Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trust Condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average willingness to pay than Safety Condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay in the Safety Condition exceeds the Trust Condition by at least 10% (EUR), conclude T1 is supported. If the Trust Condition exceeds the Safety Condition by at least 10%, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10%, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Jotun already serves individual buyers directly and has a marine protection reputation, but demand for decorative products remains soft. Conduct the proposed digital messaging test to validate whether marine protection messaging drives purchases before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.

Alternatives include expanding into consumer markets, targeting a different customer group, or maintaining current B2B focus.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential marine safety, outdoor equipment protection) using Jotun’s marine technology.
2) Expand into consumer markets without a differentiated proposition, targeting individual buyers directly with existing coatings.

assumptions: Individual buyers are willing to pay more for a brand they trust for marine protection.

The market size for individual marine and homeowner coatings is sufficient to justify investment.
predictions: A survey of individual boat owners and homeowners would show at least 30% indicating they would purchase Jotun products if priced competitively.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test for Marine vs Decorative Messaging
X1.method: Run a targeted online ad campaign with two versions: Version A presents marine protection messaging (safety, durability, trust) and Version B presents decorative design messaging (aesthetic, personalization, style). Track click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (purchase or sign-up) for each version.
X1.sample: Estimated 5,000 unique visitors (2,000 per version) from a panel of homeowners and boat owners in Scandinavia, recruited via social media and search ads.
X1.measure: CTR for each version and conversion rate (purchase or sign-up) for Version B.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Version A will achieve a higher CTR and conversion rate than Version B, indicating that marine protection messaging drives purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Version B will achieve a higher CTR and conversion rate than Version A, indicating that decorative design messaging drives purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If Version A CTR >= Version B CTR + 5 percentage points AND Version A conversion rate >= Version B conversion rate + 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on marine protection. If Version B CTR >= Version A CTR + 5 percentage points AND Version B conversion rate >= Version A conversion rate + 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on decorative design. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and maintain current B2B focus.

Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Marine vs Residential
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Marine Group (Jotun’s marine and protective coatings) or Residential Group (Jotun’s decorative and protective coatings). Each group sees a product description and a price point. The Marine Group also sees a brief explanation of Jotun’s marine technology and brand reputation. The Residential Group sees the same product description and price point without the marine explanation. Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (if any).
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 marine enthusiasts and 250 homeowners, recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay more than the baseline price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Marine Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Residential Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Residential Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Marine Group.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Marine Group is at least 5 points higher than for Residential Group (i.e., Marine ≥ 5.5 and Residential < 5.5), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 5 points, conclude neither theory is strongly supported. If both groups’ intent scores are within 5 points of each other, conclude no significant difference.

final.next_action: Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for marine versus residential messaging, and use the results to decide whether to launch a differentiated marine consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the marine enthusiast market and their willingness to pay a premium for Jotun’s products are uncertain. Additionally, the strength of direct-to-consumer sales through Jotun’s website remains unproven.
would_change_if: If the Consumer Messaging Test shows that homeowners express higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than marine enthusiasts, the recommendation would shift toward a broader residential consumer proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated marine‑focused consumer proposition targeting individual boat owners, leveraging Jotun’s marine‑grade reputation and professional endorsement. Begin with a limited pilot offering to validate demand before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, not just speculate.
Consider existing consumer reach of Jotun’s coatings; if none, assess feasibility of entering that market.
Alternatives include expanding into consumer markets, targeting a different customer group, or maintaining current B2B focus.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., residential marine safety, outdoor equipment protection) using Jotun’s marine technology.
2) Expand into consumer markets without a differentiated proposition, targeting individual buyers directly with existing coatings.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on B2B shipyards, ship owners, and industrial customers.
4) Partner with or license Jotun’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Jotun’s own brand.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a marine‑focused product description or a decorative‑focused product description, followed by a purchase intent question.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 self‑identified individual boat owners and 250 self‑identified homeowners, recruited via panel to match age, gender, and geographic distribution.
X1.measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this product?” and willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of marine‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the decorative‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of decorative‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the marine‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).

X1.decision_rule: If the marine‑exposed group’s purchase intent rate exceeds the decorative‑exposed group’s rate by at least 5 percentage points and its WTP is at least €50 higher, proceed with a marine‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite holds, proceed with a decorative‑focused proposition. If both groups’ intent rates are equal and neither meets the 5‑point difference, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, purchase behaviour, or market conditions for marine or decorative coatings. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.uncertainty: The size of the individual boat owner market and their willingness to pay a premium for marine performance are uncertain. The test will resolve whether demand exists and is sufficient to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 20% or willingness‑to‑pay below €50 for a marine‑focused product, we would reconsider the marine proposition and explore alternative consumer segments.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, providing measurable body-fat insights. This aligns with existing consumer scale adoption in Japan and the company’s medical evidence base.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.
Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).
4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Health Monitoring vs Fitness Tracking
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Health Monitoring Scale - marketed as a body-fat tracking device providing measurable insights (e.g., fat percentage, fat distribution). (2) Fitness Tracking Scale - marketed as a real-time activity and weight loss tracking device.
X1.sample: 500 adults aged 18-55, recruited from a panel in Japan and the United States, balanced for gender and BMI to reflect target markets.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Health Monitoring Scale compared to the Fitness Tracking Scale.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Fitness Tracking Scale compared to the Health Monitoring Scale.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the Health Monitoring Scale exceeds the average purchase intent for the Fitness Tracking Scale by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conduct a follow-up test to explore the fitness tracking concept.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, providing measurable body-fat insights. This aligns with existing consumer scale adoption in Japan and the company’s medical evidence base.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers aged 18‑55 who seek to monitor weight and body composition at home.
final.value_proposition: A premium‑priced home scale that delivers clear, actionable body-fat data, enabling informed health decisions and tracking progress.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 adults, 6 weeks, €15,000) to compare health‑monitoring and fitness‑tracking concepts. Use the 1.5‑point decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a health‑monitoring focused product.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for health‑monitoring insights. If the difference in purchase intent is less than 1.5 points, the fitness‑tracking concept may be explored.
would_change_if: If the test shows the fitness‑tracking concept achieving a 1.5‑point advantage over health‑monitoring, the recommendation would shift to a fitness‑tracking focused consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for real‑time activity and weight data, the recommendation would be revised to prioritize a fitness‑tracking focused product.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Health Monitoring vs Fitness Tracking
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Health Monitoring Scale - marketed as a body-fat tracking device providing measurable insights (e.g., fat percentage, fat distribution). (2) Fitness Tracking Scale - marketed as a real-time activity and weight loss tracking device.
arguments.sample: 500 adults aged 18-55, recruited from a panel in Japan and the United States, balanced for gender and BMI to reflect target markets.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Health Monitoring Scale compared to the Fitness Tracking Scale.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Fitness Tracking Scale compared to the Health Monitoring Scale.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the Health Monitoring Scale exceeds the average purchase intent for the Fitness Tracking Scale by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conduct a follow-up test to explore the fitness tracking concept.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, providing measurable body-fat insights. This aligns with existing consumer scale adoption in Japan and the company’s medical evidence base.

arguments.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers aged 18‑55 who seek to monitor weight and body composition at home.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium‑priced home scale that delivers clear, actionable body-fat data, enabling informed health decisions and tracking progress.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 adults, 6 weeks, €15,000) to compare health‑monitoring and fitness‑tracking concepts. Use the 1.5‑point decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a health‑monitoring focused product.
arguments.uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for health‑monitoring insights. If the difference in purchase intent is less than 1.5 points, the fitness‑tracking concept may be explored.
would_change_if: If the test shows the fitness‑tracking concept achieving a 1.5‑point advantage over health‑monitoring, the recommendation would shift to a fitness‑tracking focused consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for real‑time activity and weight data, the recommendation would be revised to prioritize a fitness‑tracking focused product.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness or general consumer offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, and the company already markets a professional body-fat analyser. A health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and provides a clear value proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.
Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).
4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

X1.name: Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).
X1.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Framing condition is at least 10 points higher than in the Fitness Framing condition (p < 0.05), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 10 points, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness or general consumer offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, and the company already markets a professional body-fat analyser. A health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and provides a clear value proposition.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious adults who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data for weight management.
final.value_proposition: A home body-fat analyser marketed as a health monitoring tool, providing a clear, measurable body-fat percentage to help users track weight and make informed health decisions.
final.next_action: Run the proposed framing test (300 health-conscious adults, randomized messaging, purchase intent and willingness to pay) to validate the health-framing hypothesis before committing to product development.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers will pay a premium for a health-focused device and whether the framing difference is statistically significant. Without the test, the demand for a consumer proposition remains uncertain.
would_change_if: If the framing test shows the Fitness Framing condition outperforms the Health Framing condition by at least 10 points (p < 0.05), we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore a fitness-focused approach.
If the test shows no significant difference between framing conditions, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

X1.name: Home Body Fat Analyser Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a health-focused message emphasizing body fat as a health metric for weight management; Group B receives a fitness-focused message emphasizing weight loss and activity tracking. Both groups are offered a mock home body-fat analyser at a price of €199. The primary outcome is purchase intent (binary: would purchase). Secondary outcomes include stated willingness to pay and perceived accuracy.
X1.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced across gender and age. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and stated willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for Group A exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed with a health-focused consumer proposition. If purchase intent for Group B exceeds Group A by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a fitness-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is below 10 percentage points, no expansion is recommended.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (weight management) using a home body-fat analyser, leveraging the existing consumer scale market in Japan and the health monitoring demand. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data, and the Tanita brand is already a household name in Japan.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious households in Japan and other markets where bathroom scales are common, particularly those interested in tracking weight and body composition for health improvement.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced home body-fat analyser that provides a clear, measurable health metric (body fat percentage) for weight management, supported by the Tanita brand reputation for precision and reliability.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Home Body Fat Analyser Messaging Test (or a similar experiment) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay for a health-focused versus fitness-focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. The test will resolve whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for a health-focused device.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the fitness-focused message significantly higher than for the health-focused message, the recommendation would shift to a fitness-focused consumer proposition.
If the test shows purchase intent below 10 percentage points for either messaging, no expansion would be recommended.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.

Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).

predictions: A survey of target consumers would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a home body-fat scale for weight management.

X1.name: Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 500 participants (250 self-identified health-conscious adults and 250 professional users: clinics/health clubs). Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A (health-focused) or Condition B (professional-focused). Both conditions present a home body-fat scale with identical features (foot-to-foot BIA, 1993 model). Condition A messaging emphasizes health benefits and personal wellness; Condition B messaging emphasizes clinical accuracy and professional compatibility. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).
X1.sample: 500 participants (250 health-conscious adults and 250 professional users) recruited via online panels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition A willingness to pay ≥ Condition B willingness to pay, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition B willingness to pay ≥ Condition A willingness to pay, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or professional recommendation, so it does not affect T1.

final.target_customer: Health-conscious adults and individuals seeking to manage weight and improve health, particularly in markets where body composition tracking is already common (e.g., Japan and the US).
final.value_proposition: A home body-fat scale that provides clear, actionable health insights, leveraging Tanita’s proven clinical accuracy and brand trust to differentiate from generic consumer scales.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test (Condition A vs Condition B) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay, and use the results to decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch.
final.uncertainty: The willingness to pay for a home body-fat scale in 1993 is unknown; the test could reveal price sensitivity or demand gaps. Additionally, the test does not address professional recommendation or clinical accuracy concerns, which could be a
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or willingness to pay significantly below the premium price, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion or a different consumer proposition.

If new evidence shows strong professional demand for a consumer version or that the consumer version cannot meet clinical accuracy standards, the recommendation would shift toward expanding the B2B market or licensing the technology.
If the test confirms that professional users would recommend a consumer version to colleagues, the recommendation would shift toward positioning the product as a professional-grade tool for home use.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 500 participants (250 self-identified health-conscious adults and 250 professional users: clinics/health clubs). Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A (health-focused) or Condition B (professional-focused). Both conditions present a home body-fat scale with identical features (foot-to-foot BIA, 1993 model). Condition A messaging emphasizes health benefits and personal wellness; Condition B messaging emphasizes clinical accuracy and professional compatibility. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).
arguments.sample: 500 participants (250 health-conscious adults and 250 professional users) recruited via online panels.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.

arguments.decision_rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition A willingness to pay ≥ Condition B willingness to pay, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition B willingness to pay ≥ Condition A willingness to pay, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home use, emphasizing health benefits and personal wellness. The evidence shows strong consumer demand for health-focused devices (household scales are common, and health concerns are prominent) and Tanita’s existing professional credibility. A test could validate willingness to pay and purchase intent, but the current evidence supports T1 as the most plausible path

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness or general consumer offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, and the company already markets a professional body-fat analyser. A health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and provides a clear value proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.
Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).
4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits to home users.

X1.name: Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).
X1.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Framing condition is at least 10 points higher than in the Fitness Framing condition (p < 0.05), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 10 points, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, pricing, or purchase behavior for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it does not affect the theory.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness or general consumer offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, and the company already markets a professional body-fat analyser. A health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and provides a clear value proposition.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious adults who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data for weight management.
final.value_proposition: A home body-fat analyser marketed as a health monitoring tool that provides a clear, measurable body-fat percentage, enabling users to track weight and body composition for informed health decisions.
final.next_action: Run the proposed framing test (300 health-conscious adults, randomized messaging, purchase intent and willingness to pay) to validate the health-framing hypothesis before committing to product development.
final.uncertainty: The test results are pending; without actual purchase data, the actual demand and willingness to pay for a health-focused home body-fat analyser remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the framing test shows a purchase intent difference of less than 10 points between the Health and Fitness framings, indicating no significant advantage for either framing, the recommendation would shift to no expansion and continued B2B

If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for fitness tracking or that consumers are willing to pay a premium for a fitness-focused device, the recommendation would shift toward a fitness-focused consumer proposition

arguments.name: Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).
arguments.sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Framing condition is at least 10 points higher than in the Fitness Framing condition (p < 0.05), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 10 points, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness or general consumer offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, and the company already markets a professional body-fat analyser. A health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and provides a clear value proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for weight management, leveraging Tanita’s existing health messaging and the established household scale market. The evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and seek health insights, making a health‑focused positioning likely to drive purchase.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.
Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).
4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, because they already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health insights.
T1.who_benefits: Home users who want to track weight and body composition for health improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a health tool, consumers will be motivated to purchase it for regular use, increasing purchase frequency.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing for a health-focused device, and potential subscription services for data analysis.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a device that provides measurable health insights.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits of the device.
The device is accurate enough to provide meaningful health information.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will express intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser if marketed as a health monitoring tool.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public sources from 2002 indicate the 406 MHz PLB is intended for life‑threatening remote emergencies and is regulated for general public use, but there is no evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market feasibility. The proposed test (X1) would be needed to validate whether consumers will adopt a premium, life‑saving positioning.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a life-saving emergency device for remote environments, and they will purchase it if it is positioned as a premium safety tool for outdoor activities (e.g., hiking, camping, boating).
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers will shift from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they understand its unique capability to reach a distress call through satellite, offering peace of mind and higher perceived safety.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling premium-priced units directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online channels, leveraging its existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of the existence and purpose of 406 MHz PLBs.
Outdoor activities in remote areas (e.g., Alaska, Australia) are common enough to create demand.
Willingness to pay a premium for a specialized device is higher than for generic ELTs.
ACR can reach individual buyers through existing channels or new partnerships.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused marketing campaign to outdoor groups, purchase intent will exceed 10% among respondents who identify themselves as hikers, campers, or boating recreationists.
Surveyed consumers will cite 'safety in remote emergencies' as the top reason for purchasing the beacon, with willingness to pay at least $800.
T1.first_claim: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a life-saving emergency device for remote environments, and they will purchase it if it is positioned as a premium safety tool for outdoor activities (e.g., hiking, camping, boating).

T2.claim: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a cost-effective, no‑regulation alternative to expensive ELTs and RFFI, and they will purchase it when price is the primary barrier to entry.
T2.who_benefits: Budget‑conscious outdoor enthusiasts, boat owners, and emergency‑prepared individuals who need a reliable signaling device without the cost of professional certification.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers will switch from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they perceive it as a cheaper, simpler solution that meets the same safety requirement without the regulatory and certification overhead.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling lower‑priced units through mass‑market channels, leveraging its existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑focused version of its existing product line.
assumptions: Price is the primary barrier to adoption for emergency signaling devices.
Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz PLBs but do not view them as a premium product.
ACR can produce a consumer‑grade version of its existing product at a lower cost than its current B2B offerings.
predictions: In a test offering a low‑priced consumer version of the beacon, purchase intent will be higher among respondents who cite budget constraints as their primary reason for not buying a beacon.
Surveyed consumers will cite 'cost' as the top reason for not purchasing a beacon, with willingness to pay at least $500.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs. Cost-Concern Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 400 respondents (200 self-identified outdoor enthusiasts/hikers, 200 budget-conscious consumers). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: (A) premium positioning emphasizing life-saving capability and remote emergency use; (B) cost‑concern positioning emphasizing lower price and no certification requirement. Both conditions present a $800 price point for a consumer‑grade 406 MHz beacon. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).
X1.sample: 400 respondents (200 outdoor enthusiasts, 200 budget‑conscious consumers) recruited via outdoor forums and general consumer panels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and at least 5% among budget‑conscious consumers; primary reason will be "safety in remote emergencies."
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the cost‑concern condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and at least 5% among outdoor enthusiasts; primary reason will be "cost."

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the cost‑concern condition exceeds 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, consider a lower‑priced consumer version. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public sources from 2002 indicate the 406 MHz PLB is intended for life‑threatening remote emergencies and is regulated for general public use, but there is no evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market feasibility. The proposed test (X1) would be needed to validate whether consumers will adopt a premium, life‑saving positioning.
final.target_customer: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product positioned as a premium safety tool for remote emergencies, leveraging ACR’s existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under premium and cost‑concern messaging conditions.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers through existing channels remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.
If the test shows purchase intent in the cost‑concern condition exceeds 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, we would consider a lower‑priced consumer version.
If neither condition meets its threshold, we would maintain the current focus on B2B customers and existing product portfolio.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs. Cost-Concern Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 400 respondents (200 self-identified outdoor enthusiasts/hikers, 200 budget-conscious consumers). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: (A) premium positioning emphasizing life-saving capability and remote emergency use; (B) cost‑concern positioning emphasizing lower price and no certification requirement. Both conditions present a $800 price point for a consumer‑grade 406 MHz beacon. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).
arguments.sample: 400 respondents (200 outdoor enthusiasts, 200 budget‑conscious consumers) recruited via outdoor forums and general consumer panels.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and at least 5% among budget‑conscious consumers; primary reason will be "safety in remote emergencies."
prediction_by_theory.T2: In the cost‑concern condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and at least 5% among outdoor enthusiasts; primary reason will be "cost."

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the cost‑concern condition exceeds 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, consider a lower‑priced consumer version. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher among respondents who cite safety and emergency signaling as primary reason, and higher in regions with high outdoor recreation participation.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for T1 exceeds purchase intent for T2 by at least 10 percentage points among respondents who cite safety as primary reason, proceed with a consumer proposition focused on safety necessity. If purchase intent for T2 exceeds T1 by at least 10 percentage points among respondents who cite status as primary reason, proceed with a premium positioning proposition. If neither difference meets the 10‑point threshold, do not expand into a consumer proposition and continue focusing on B2B customers.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. final.uncertainty: Consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer‑grade 406 MHz PLB are uncertain; the test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for T2 (status/premium positioning) exceeding T1 by at least 10 percentage points among respondents who cite status as primary reason, we would reconsider a premium positioning proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

X1.name: Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Consumer Group (target marine recreational users) or Professional Group (target commercial marine users). Each group sees a product description of a 406 MHz consumer-grade distress beacon, but the key difference is the framing: Consumer Group receives a message emphasizing personal safety, affordability, and ease of use for recreational users; Professional Group receives a message emphasizing professional reliability, compliance with RTCM standards, and suitability for commercial marine operations.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users (recruited via outdoor recreation forums and social media) and 150 commercial marine users (recruited via maritime trade associations and professional networks).
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Professional Group, because the message frames the product as a personal safety item for recreational users.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Consumer Group, because the message frames the product as a professional-grade, compliance‑oriented device for commercial marine users.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent of the Consumer Group is at least 1.5 points higher than that of the Professional Group (i.e., Consumer Group average >= Professional Group average + 1.5), we conclude that T1 is more likely and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude that T2 is more likely and recommend no expansion.

Public sources show ACR's 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use and meets regulatory requirements, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay. final.target_customer: Marine recreational users who face unplanned emergencies at sea.
final.value_proposition: A lightweight, affordable 406 MHz distress beacon that meets safety standards and is available through consumer retailers, offering reliable marine safety for recreational users.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test (300 respondents, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand, price sensitivity, and willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon are uncertain. The test will resolve whether marine recreational users would adopt a lower-priced, consumer-focused product.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer beacon are significantly lower than for professional marine equipment, we would reconsider expansion and explore alternative routes to market.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand or a large market for marine recreational safety devices, we would reconsider investing in a differentiated consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.

X1.name: Status vs. Emergency Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
X1.sample: 200 marine recreational users recruited via outdoor recreation forums and social media, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willing to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% will report purchasing for status reasons, and 15% will pay $500+ for a consumer-grade beacon.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 20% will report purchasing for status reasons, and 15% will pay $500+ for a consumer-grade beacon.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents who cite status reasons exceeds 20% and the average willingness to pay for status-driven purchases is at least $500, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing status and brand prestige. If the proportion of status-driven purchases is below 20% or the average willingness to pay is below $300, focus on an emergency-driven proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer purchase motivations for a satellite distress beacon. Therefore it provides no support or contradiction to T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. final.next_action: Run the 8‑week online survey test (200 marine users, €15k budget) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for status vs. emergency messaging.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before late 2002, and no source shows individual buyers purchase for status reasons or that status drives demand. The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) provides no support for T1.
would_change_if: If the test shows at least 20% of respondents cite status reasons and an average willingness to pay of $500 or more, we would reconsider a status‑driven consumer proposition.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: The Federal Register rule (2002) and NOAA guidelines make compliance mandatory, creating a regulatory barrier that only a certified device can clear, prompting consumers to choose a trusted brand over generic alternatives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium-priced, certified product through retail channels, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and the FCC waiver that allowed type certification for consumer use.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Emergency vs Tracking Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing life-saving emergency capability (NOAA certification, RTCM compliance, suitable for remote or life-threatening situations). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes continuous tracking and real-time rescue notifications (GPS, location updates, rescue alerts). Both groups see a price point 20% above a generic PLB (e.g., €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state the primary purchase driver.
X1.sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across gender and age to reflect marine recreational and outdoor user demographics. Recruitment targets individuals who have used a personal locator beacon or are interested in emergency safety gear.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase driver (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (price sensitivity).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, and the majority of Group A buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Group A, and the majority of Group B buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary drivers.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than Group B, adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition (emergency capability). If Group B purchase intent ≥ 20% points higher than Group A, adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition (tracking/continuous). If the difference is ≤ 10% points, no expansion is recommended. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or tracking capabilities for a 406 MHz satellite distress beacon. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR already sells to individual buyers (e.g., marine recreational users) and has a B2B reputation, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for tracking or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed test to measure purchase intent differences between emergency and tracking messaging.
final.target_customer: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that meets NOAA/RTCM certification, offering life-saving emergency capability and compliance with regulatory requirements, sold through retail channels at a premium price.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Proposition Test (Emergency vs Tracking Messaging) within the 12‑week, €18,000 budget to measure purchase intent differences and determine whether to pursue a consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium for certification, and the competitive landscape for consumer PLBs are uncertain. The test will clarify these points.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the emergency messaging group at least 15% higher than for the tracking messaging group, we would adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition.

If neither condition is met and the difference is ≤ 10% points, we would recommend no expansion.

result.question: It is late 2002. Should ACR Electronics develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology? What evidence would justify that investment?
result.brief: ACR Electronics is a Fort Lauderdale maker of emergency radio beacons for ships and aircraft and of survival lights for military and commercial marine users. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

arguments.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging ACR’s 406 MHz satellite technology. The evidence shows ACR already sells a consumer‑grade PLB (GyPSI 406) and that outdoor enthusiasts have benefited from successful rescues, but the purchase mechanism (NOAA registration, FCC approval) remains a barrier. A test offering a consumer‑grade PLB at $700, with a brief explanation

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.
Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales.

T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who face remote emergency situations and want reliable rescue communication.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from relying on traditional PLBs (registered with NOAA) to a consumer product that meets FCC approval and offers real-time rescue capability, reducing fear of being unreachable.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price (e.g., $700) through retail channels, capturing margin on a single-use device rather than recurring B2B services.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. are sufficient to generate a meaningful consumer market.
FCC approval and NOAA registration requirements do not deter consumers from purchasing a consumer product.
Marketing can effectively communicate the safety benefit to individual buyers.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade PLB to outdoor enthusiasts, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a B2B version of the same technology.
Surveyed buyers will cite 'emergency rescue' as the primary reason for purchase, not cost or compatibility with existing gear.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
